verdicts.evidence: The emitted bytes are a function of the listing order: measured by replacing `.sort()` with `.sort().reverse()`, all three readiness drafts and the OSCAL change (`Addressed by rules: frontier-deterministic-boundary, hexa-move-deterministic-out, security-prompt-injection` comes out reversed). `.sort()` is the only thing making that order independent of the filesystem. POSIX does not define readdir order and ext4's htree returns hash order, so two runs on identical artifacts on two machines emit different bytes for the OSCAL a GRC tool ingests - under a header that says "Assembled ... deterministically" and beside `detUuid`, which exists precisely so "two runs on the same artifacts produce byte-identical OSCAL". The code comment states the invariant in the same words. Recipe on ext4: delete and re-create one file in `runward/rules/` (any editor rewrite), re-run `runward compliance` - the entry moves in readdir order and the pack's bytes move with it, with no change of content. NOT reproduced here, and the reason matters: APFS returns directory entries in lexicographic order, so this defect is invisible on the maintainer's laptop, and `test/unit/oscal-golden.test.js` only compares two runs on one machine and one filesystem - which is why it survived. Filed as a hole against the determinism claim, not against the content.

verdicts.evidence: Surface: the membership of `ComplianceInputs.rules`, the array. The array's single consumer is `if (asiCoverage.has(id))` in `gatherComplianceInputs`, and that map's keys are exactly `Object.keys(ASI_LABELS)` = ASI01..ASI10, all of which already satisfy `/^ASI\d{2}$/`. Dropping the filter can only ADMIT tokens that are not ASI ids; it cannot remove one - so the coverage map, and every artifact derived from it, is unreachable by this mutation.
